To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

drug firms offer price discounts to health care plans to avoid being off-listed, that price discounts do not cause prices outside managed care to rise, and that price caps affect the way prices evolve over time.

(1) drug firms offer discounts and other forms of price discrimination to managed care organizations to avoid going off-formulary; and (2) price caps cause prices to be lower at the time of entry, but higher over time.

1) discounts obtained by health providers do not cause price increases outside managed care, and 2) price caps cause drug firms to set higher introductory prices but raise them less dramatically over time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of formularies on the incentives of pharmaceutical firms.
the effect of managed care and formularies on the prices charged by pharmaceutical firms, and on the evolution of these prices over time.
the effects of formularies and price caps on the pricing strategies of drug firms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the formulary system and price caps have a limited effect on drug prices.

price differentials caused by the formulary system are not caused by price differentials caused in the market outside the formulary system, but rather that the formulary system is a mechanism to keep prices low.
drug price differentials caused by formularies and price caps are not necessarily harmful for the welfare of patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
drug firms are willing to offer discounts to health providers to avoid being excluded from formularies, but they are not willing to offer discounts outside managed care.
the threat of going off-list causes prices to be higher than they would otherwise be.

price caps are not the right instrument to address drug price differentials, and that the threat of being excluded from the formularies of health care providers is the main driver of price differentials.
The main takeaway from our work is that
drug firms are able to pass on discounts to consumers, but only when competing in monopolistically competitive markets.
the behaviour of drug prices is affected by the threat of exclusion from the formulary, and this effect is amplified when price caps are introduced.
formularies can be used to control prices and that this can be done in an economically efficient manner.
